messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aamir Rahman was 49, a married South Asian military medic who had spent most of his adult life training himself to stay composed under pressure, so it felt especially disorienting to him when the abuse from a former romantic partner began to live on inside him long after the relationship ended. The relationship had turned frightening in private ways that left little evidence for anyone else to see, and what still reached him most vividly were narrow, sensory fragments: the sour smell of sweat or body odour in a crowded room, the sight of police uniforms near his workplace or in the neighbourhood, and even reminders of related people whose presence seemed to pull the whole ordeal back into the room with him. When any of these appeared, he would tense before he could think, and his first reaction was to pull away from people altogether, avoid exercise classes or gym spaces where bodies and sweat were unavoidable, and stop wearing similar clothes because the fabric and fit seemed to carry the memory of what had happened to him. He could not help linking those reminders to the belief that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, that the people responsible had faced no consequences, and that there was something wrong with him as a person for having lived through it and still feeling so altered by it.

Those appraisals did not stay abstract. Aamir had come to believe that if no one had been held accountable, then the world remained fundamentally unsafe and he needed to stay on guard, especially at night, when he lay awake watching the door and listening for sounds. He described difficulty falling asleep because he felt he had to stay alert, and ordinary noises in the house would make him jump in a way that embarrassed him and then made him more watchful still. He increasingly felt safe only in a very limited number of places, and the smaller that safe zone became, the more he avoided other people, including colleagues after work and friends who had once been easy company. At the same time, the memory itself would intrude: when he tried to explain what had happened, he said he could not put it into words, but once a cue got hold of him, the event returned with such force that it felt like it was happening right now. In those moments his body reacted before his mind could organize the scene, and he felt physical pain in the same parts of his body that had been hurt during the abuse, as if the past had reactivated in flesh as much as in thought. The memory then fed back into his negative view of himself and the world, confirming for him that he was damaged and that what happened had gone unanswered, which made him even more convinced he should keep to himself and keep scanning for danger.

Over the months after the relationship ended, those protective habits began to run his life. He avoided people whenever he could, turned down invitations, and at work kept interactions brief, especially in the clinic and locker room where body odour and close proximity could catch him off guard. He stopped exercising, partly because exertion made him feel exposed in his body and partly because he feared the familiar shame and panic that could follow if the memory returned mid-workout. Yet the more he withdrew and tried to control what he wore and where he went, the smaller his world became, and that narrowing seemed to deepen his belief that something was fundamentally wrong with him and that life had lost its purpose. The avoidance also kept him from testing whether he was truly safe, so the sense that danger might be around any corner remained intact; he stayed keyed up, more easily startled, and more likely to interpret ordinary sounds or the approach of police as signs that something bad was about to happen. Even the act of avoiding could bring the memories closer, because removing himself from people and from familiar routines left him alone with the images and bodily sensations. When he later found himself in a room with a relative connected to the old relationship, the reminder was enough to make the scene flash back with painful immediacy, and afterward he would withdraw further, ashamed of how quickly the fear had taken over.

By the time Aamir sought help, he was exhausted by the cycle of sleepless vigilance, shrinking comfort, and the sense that his life had been emptied out by what others had done to him. What finally brought him in was a recent evening in which a smell of sweat in a crowded place, a nearby police officer, and the presence of a related person all seemed to converge at once, leaving him shaking, physically hurting, and unable to calm himself afterward. He was not only afraid that the abuse could live on in his body and mind indefinitely, but also afraid that if he continued this way, he would end up with nothing left that felt meaningful.
